correctness.rationale: The defining finite one-point game has q colour types over zero or one marked point, and q times the number of oriented cyclic gaps over two or more marked points; exact induction therefore yields the displayed three-case min/max recurrence. The linear-gap multiplicity lemma (rank s requires 2^s-1 instances of each colour) is proved by a central-pivot induction. Choosing first and second extensions of the same challenged colour forces 2^(t-1) of that colour in every rank-t cyclic host, for each colour. Periodic q-colour permutation words of q*2^(t-1) points meet the bound: for any first challenge and any second challenged colour, a second point in the opposite q-block leaves each arc containing q*(2^(t-2)-1) periodic symbols, hence a linear gap of rank >=t-2. The eight-point census has ten exhaustive balanced binary necklace representatives, nine with explicit split-arc witness indices, one two-run obstruction; orbit sizes are 2,4 and seven 8s. An independently coded subset-by-subset game and the gap evaluator agreed on all masks for 1616 words, and the full eight-point balanced stratum gave 62 positive words / 9 rotation classes. This is a complete proof, not extrapolation from finite experiments.

value.rationale: A canonical Fraïssé class (oriented cyclic orders with named colours) has a genuine low-cardinality type discontinuity not covered by the ordinary linear gap theorem. The exact relative-rank algorithm and universal per-colour minimal size q*2^(t-1) solve a natural all-level extremal invariant with no arbitrary parameter slice. The binary rank-three equality boundary further demonstrates that count balance alone ceases to suffice: among 10 minimum-size balanced necklaces only the two-run type fails, leaving 9 rotation types. Both the structural two-arc condition and the complete natural first-obstruction census are reusable for studies of rank games and cyclic orders; no inflated general theorem is inferred.
